variants.title: Build a LIME surrogate
variants.context: LIME does not decompose the model. It defines an interpretable representation, samples plausible neighbors around the case, weights them by proximity and fits a simple surrogate, then measures how well that surrogate reproduces the black box in that neighborhood.
variants.prompt: An analyst wants a local explanation for one declined loan application. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Report weighted local fidelity, seed stability, neighborhood coverage, and the configuration that produced them.
Define the interpretable representation, such as tabular bins or grouped domain features.
Query the black box on those neighbors, apply the proximity kernel, and fit a sparse linear surrogate.
Generate perturbed neighbors that respect types, constraints, and the production support.

variants.hint: What has to be defined before anything can be perturbed?
variants.explanation: The surrogate's coefficients mean nothing until fidelity in the weighted neighborhood has been measured and reported.

variants.title: Build a LIME surrogate
variants.context: LIME does not decompose the model. It defines an interpretable representation, samples plausible neighbors around the case, weights them by proximity and fits a simple surrogate, then measures how well that surrogate reproduces the black box in that neighborhood.
variants.prompt: A reviewer asks which phrases drove a text moderation decision. Put the steps in order for that case.

items.text: Score each neighbor with the moderation model, weight by proximity, and fit the sparse surrogate.
Check that the surrogate reproduces the model in that neighborhood before quoting any phrase as influential.
Create neighbors by deleting or masking those units so the fragments remain text the model could see.
Choose tokens and phrases as the interpretable units the explanation is allowed to talk about.

variants.hint: Different representations ask materially different questions.
variants.explanation: Token deletion, category bins, and engineered features are different questions, so the representation choice is part of the claim.

variants.title: Build a LIME surrogate
variants.context: LIME does not decompose the model. It defines an interpretable representation, samples plausible neighbors around the case, weights them by proximity and fits a simple surrogate, then measures how well that surrogate reproduces the black box in that neighborhood.
variants.prompt: Two seeds produce different top features for the same case. Put the steps in order and end with what the gate does.

items.text: Each run fits its surrogate and reports weighted local fidelity next to its coefficients.
The gate compares signs and top-feature overlap across seeds and blocks the payload when they disagree.
The frozen contract fixes the representation, kernel width, and sparsity for both runs.
Each run samples its own neighborhood from that same perturbation rule.

variants.hint: Which comparison is only possible once both runs have reported?
variants.explanation: A seed change under a frozen contract should not reorder important features, so disagreement blocks release rather than being averaged away.

variants.title: Route an explanation request
variants.context: A production explanation is a governed pipeline. The decision service returns the prediction and its versions, an orchestrator authorizes and routes the request, explainer workers compute and validate the evidence, and an evidence store keeps the immutable payload the audience finally sees.
variants.prompt: A customer contests a decision and an agent requests an explanation. Put the pipeline stages in order.

items.text: The orchestrator selects the approved contract for this audience, enforces budgets, and takes a consistent feature snapshot.
The evidence store keeps the immutable payload and the interface renders only audience-appropriate features and caveats.
The decision service returns the model output and records model, feature, calibration, and policy versions.
An explainer worker loads the pinned model and reference, generates evidence, and checks fidelity or reconciliation.

variants.hint: Which stage must not wait for heavy explanation work?
variants.explanation: Separating prediction from explanation keeps an expensive query off the decision path and keeps every artifact versioned.

variants.title: Route an explanation request
variants.context: A production explanation is a governed pipeline. The decision service returns the prediction and its versions, an orchestrator authorizes and routes the request, explainer workers compute and validate the evidence, and an evidence store keeps the immutable payload the audience finally sees.
variants.prompt: A model rollout is in progress while an explanation job runs. Put the stages in order, keeping versions from mixing.

items.text: The stored payload names the pinned versions, so a rerun can reproduce the same evidence later.
The prediction is served and its exact model and feature versions are recorded with the trace identifier.
The orchestrator pins the model and background artifacts for the whole job before routing it.
The worker computes against those pinned artifacts so no mid-job upgrade can change the reference.

variants.hint: What would happen if the artifacts were resolved twice?
variants.explanation: Pinning model and background artifacts for the full job prevents a rollout from mixing versions inside one explanation.

variants.title: Route an explanation request
variants.context: A production explanation is a governed pipeline. The decision service returns the prediction and its versions, an orchestrator authorizes and routes the request, explainer workers compute and validate the evidence, and an evidence store keeps the immutable payload the audience finally sees.
variants.prompt: The explainer exceeds its latency budget for a synchronous request. Put the stages in order, ending with the fallback.

items.text: The system falls back to a plain decision notice or human review and records the failed attempt.
The decision service has already returned the output and its versions to the caller.
The worker exceeds the profiled bound and fails its gate rather than returning a partial ranking.
The orchestrator enforces the request budget and rate limit for this audience.

variants.hint: What is the safe output when the gate cannot be met?
variants.explanation: Never show an unvalidated partial ranking, because a plausible chart that failed its gate is worse than no chart.

variants.title: Reconcile the additive explanation
variants.context: A local additive explanation states that the explained output equals the base value plus the sum of the feature contributions. Local accuracy means that reconstruction has to recover the model output on the same scale, within the method's numerical tolerance.
variants.prompt: A SHAP payload reports a base value of 0.30 and three contributions: income +0.25, prior defaults -0.08, and tenure +0.12. What model output should this explanation reconcile to?
variants.hint: Add every contribution to the base value, keeping the signs.
variants.explanation: Local accuracy means base value plus all contributions recovers the explained output on the same output scale.

mistakes.feedback: That flips the negative contribution to positive, which double counts a feature that lowered the score.
That reports the sum of contributions and leaves out the base value the explanation starts from.

variants.title: Reconcile the additive explanation
variants.context: A local additive explanation states that the explained output equals the base value plus the sum of the feature contributions. Local accuracy means that reconstruction has to recover the model output on the same scale, within the method's numerical tolerance.
variants.prompt: A payload reports the explained output as 0.72, a base value of 0.40, and contributions of +0.18, +0.09, and -0.05. What is the reconciliation gap between the reported output and the reconstructed one?
variants.hint: Rebuild the output from the payload first, then compare it with what was reported.
variants.explanation: The reconciliation gap is reported output minus base value minus the sum of contributions, and a nonzero gap means the payload cannot be trusted as additive.

mistakes.feedback: That is the distance from base value to output, which is the amount to explain rather than the gap.
That is the reconstructed value itself, not its difference from the reported output.

variants.title: Reconcile the additive explanation
variants.context: A local additive explanation states that the explained output equals the base value plus the sum of the feature contributions. Local accuracy means that reconstruction has to recover the model output on the same scale, within the method's numerical tolerance.
variants.prompt: An explanation of a 0.65 score has a base value of 0.20 and shows only three of its four contributions: +0.30, -0.10, and +0.15. What must the hidden fourth contribution be for the payload to reconcile?
variants.hint: The four contributions have to close the distance between the base value and the output.
variants.explanation: Every contribution is one feature's allocated share of the difference from the base value, so the shares must sum to that difference exactly.

mistakes.feedback: That subtracts only the base value and ignores the three contributions already shown.
That treats the -0.10 contribution as positive, so the remainder is pushed the wrong way.

variants.title: Separate semantic change from noise
variants.context: Not every change in an explanation is noise. Changing the reference cohort changes the question being asked, changing a seed under a frozen contract should not reorder important features, and a larger sampling budget reduces variance without repairing unrealistic perturbations.
variants.prompt: The same prediction is explained against the full training population and then against a matched peer cohort. The base value and the top features change. What is the right reading?
options: The comparison question changed, so both explanations can be valid.
The explainer is unstable, so the sampling budget should be raised.
The model drifted between the two runs, so the run should be repeated.
optionFeedback: Correct, an attribution answers why a score differs from a reference, and a different reference is a different question.
Sampling budget addresses estimator variance, which is not what a deliberate cohort change produces.
Nothing changed in the model here, only the background population the explanation compares against.
variants.hint: What did the team actually change between the two runs?
variants.explanation: Changing the reference cohort deliberately changes the comparison question, so the two results are not interchangeable answers.

variants.title: Separate semantic change from noise
variants.context: Not every change in an explanation is noise. Changing the reference cohort changes the question being asked, changing a seed under a frozen contract should not reorder important features, and a larger sampling budget reduces variance without repairing unrealistic perturbations.
variants.prompt: Under one frozen contract, five seeds return different top features and two of them flip a coefficient sign. Prediction quality is unchanged. What should the release gate do?
options: Block the payload and raise the budget or switch to a lower-variance estimator.
Publish the average of the five explanations as the customer-facing result.
Ship the highest-fidelity seed and note the variance in the audit log.
optionFeedback: Correct, a frozen contract should not reorder important features, so this is estimator noise that has to be reduced first.
Averaging unstable runs hides the instability rather than resolving it and still ships an unrepeatable claim.
Choosing the best-looking seed is selection, not evidence, and the next request would return something else.
variants.hint: Nothing about the question changed between these runs.
variants.explanation: Repeatability is its own gate: compare signs, top-feature overlap, and rank correlation across seeds before any payload is released.

variants.title: Separate semantic change from noise
variants.context: Not every change in an explanation is noise. Changing the reference cohort changes the question being asked, changing a seed under a frozen contract should not reorder important features, and a larger sampling budget reduces variance without repairing unrealistic perturbations.
variants.prompt: An explanation perturbs income independently of occupation and location, creating records the model never sees in production. The team raises the sample count tenfold and variance drops. What is still wrong?
options: The audience is wrong, so the payload should be redacted before it is shown.
The neighborhood is unrealistic, so the extra samples only stabilize an invalid question.
The output scale is wrong, so the contributions cannot reconcile with the model output.
optionFeedback: Redaction governs disclosure, and it does not make an implausible neighborhood valid.
Correct, a larger budget reduces approximation variance but cannot repair perturbations outside the production support.
Nothing here indicates a scale mismatch, and reconciliation is a separate check from perturbation realism.
variants.hint: A stable explanation can still be the wrong one.
variants.explanation: Correlated substitutes make independent perturbation unrealistic, and sampling budget cannot fix a neighborhood the model never encounters.

variants.title: Choose the estimator
variants.context: Match the estimator to model access, scope, latency, and the validation burden the team can operate. Model-specific SHAP exploits structure, model-agnostic SHAP only needs prediction queries but costs many evaluations, LIME buys a fast local hypothesis, and an interpretable model may be the real answer.
variants.prompt: A team owns the training code for a gradient-boosted tree ensemble and needs additive contributions for every scored case. What should they use first?
options: TreeSHAP, then verify output scale, base value, and additivity after library upgrades.
Kernel SHAP, budgeting many prediction queries per case for sampling variance.
LIME with tabular bins, gating weighted local fidelity for each case.
optionFeedback: Correct, a model-specific method is the first choice when the structure is available and supported.
A model-agnostic method pays for access it does not need here and adds sampling variance.
LIME gives a local hypothesis, not the additive contributions the team asked for.
variants.hint: What model access does the team actually have?
variants.explanation: Prefer an exact or efficient model-specific method when the structure supports it, then verify scale and additivity after upgrades.

variants.title: Choose the estimator
variants.context: Match the estimator to model access, scope, latency, and the validation burden the team can operate. Model-specific SHAP exploits structure, model-agnostic SHAP only needs prediction queries but costs many evaluations, LIME buys a fast local hypothesis, and an interpretable model may be the real answer.
variants.prompt: A vendor model is reachable only through a prediction endpoint, and a regulator requires additive contributions that reconcile with the score. What fits?
options: TreeSHAP, since the vendor model is very likely a tree ensemble underneath.
A LIME surrogate, since it also produces per-feature coefficients.
A model-agnostic SHAP method, with a budget for many evaluations per case.
optionFeedback: Assuming an unverified internal structure would apply an algorithm whose assumptions cannot be checked.
LIME coefficients come from a surrogate and do not reconcile additively with the model output.
Correct, query-only access with additive semantics is exactly the model-agnostic case, and it must be budgeted.
variants.hint: Which requirement rules out a surrogate?
variants.explanation: Use model-agnostic SHAP when additive semantics matter but only prediction queries are available, and gate seed, sample, and background sensitivity.

variants.title: Choose the estimator
variants.context: Match the estimator to model access, scope, latency, and the validation burden the team can operate. Model-specific SHAP exploits structure, model-agnostic SHAP only needs prediction queries but costs many evaluations, LIME buys a fast local hypothesis, and an interpretable model may be the real answer.
variants.prompt: A lending team keeps failing repeatability gates, and what the business actually needs is a decision policy reviewers can inspect and defend. What is the better answer?
options: Raise the SHAP sampling budget until the repeatability gate passes.
Present LIME coefficients averaged across the portfolio as global importance.
Replace the black box with a monotonic model, scorecard, or small rule list.
optionFeedback: More budget can reduce variance but does not give reviewers the inspectable policy they asked for.
Averaging local surrogates into a global claim is exactly the promotion the method does not support.
Correct, when the real requirement is stable inspectable logic, an interpretable model beats explaining an opaque one.
variants.hint: Ask what the stakeholder needs, not which chart is available.
variants.explanation: Sometimes the best explanation system refuses to manufacture a ranking and routes the case to a clearer model instead.
